title: AIPAC halts endorsements and direct contributions to candidates
description: In this file photo from 2023, U.S. and I
body:
In this file photo from 2023, U.S. and Israeli flags fill a field in Boston, Massachusetts.
                
                    Joseph Prezioso/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Joseph Prezioso/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   The pro-Israel political organization AIPAC, or the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, announced on Wednesday that it will no longer issue endorsements, make direct PAC contributions or earmark funds for candidates.   A longtime influential lobbying group, AIPAC started its direct political involvement five years ago. Since then, particularly this midterm election cycle, AIPAC has been met with mounting resistance. The group has faced criticism over its stances on various issues, including the wars in Gaza and Iran.   Candidates endorsed by AIPAC have also faced tough opposition from both the political right and the political left for accepting the organization's support and financial contributions as public opinion on the U.S. relationship with Israel has shifted. In order to tame the criticism, some AIPAC-endorsed candidates said they won't accept any money from the organization.   
   AIPAC first announced the changes in a letter to members, stating "the challenges we are confronting will continue to grow in the years ahead." In the letter, AIPAC said it wouldn't stop funneling money to candidates that align with the group's mission by mobilizing individual donors.   "We will prioritize increasing direct, organized contributions from individual Americans to candidates—expanding upon our current efforts—and maximizing the emerging political fundraising tools," the letter said.   The letter added that the 2028 cycle will "demand an even stronger commitment by our activists to pro-Israel politics." As a result, the group plans to increase support "for the Republicans and Democrats who are advancing policies that strengthen America's alliance with Israel and standing up against anti-Israel legislation."   In a statement to NPR, AIPAC spokesperson Deryn Sousa said the group's mission and strategy remains the same despite the changes.     "Our goal is to build support for the U.S.-Israel relationship. AIPAC members gave more than $90 million directly to candidates this cycle, and that organized, direct giving from our members will continue and increase."   AIPAC contributed nearly $25 million to candidates and political committees in 2026 through Sept. 30, according to FEC filings. Its affiliated super PAC United Democracy Project contributed $13 million to candidates and political committees and spent an additional $53.5 million in independent expenditures.    
   AIPAC confirmed with NPR that its affiliated super PAC, United Democracy Project, will continue to operate and will be able to raise an unlimited amount of money.  It has spent heavily to support pro-Israel candidates, and oppose those who criticize Israel.    In recent days, several of the super PAC's individual independent expenditures are being used to campaign against Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Michigan.    AIPAC also spent heavily to campaign against El-Sayed in the primary, backing his opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens. The Michigan Senate contest is just one of the high-profile races where AIPAC has spent in favor of a pro-Israel politician or in opposition to someone the organization sees as less favorable to Israel.

title: Poll: Voters want Congress to be a check on Trump, trust Democrats more on issues
description: In this file photo from July 2026, Presi
body:
In this file photo from July 2026, President Trump shows off an executive order he signed in the Oval Office of the White House.
                
                    Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
    

   
   Voters have record low trust in Republicans' ability to handle their top issues like immigration and rising prices, according to the latest Strength In Numbers/Verasight poll shared with NPR.   The poll also finds a strong majority of voters want the next Congress to undo President Trump's agenda — or act as a check on his power — on policies like tariffs and trade, health care and immigration.   Less than two weeks out from Election Day, voters say they'd prefer to elect a Democrat to Congress over a Republican by a double-digit margin among registered voters (52% to 41%) and likely voters (54% to 42%).   
   The survey of 2,028 respondents was conducted Oct. 13-19 and has a margin of sampling error of 2.2 percentage points, meaning results could be about 2.2 points higher or lower.   Trump's job approval sits at near-record lows for his second term, with just 34% approving of his performance and 62% disapproving, with 50% strongly disapproving.   G. Elliott Morris, author of the Strength In Numbers newsletter and CEO of polling company Wave Polling and Research, said the latest poll explains the current challenges with the political landscape Republicans face.   "Trump's ratings hit new lows on seven of the 10 issues we've tracked since May 2025, from jobs and trade to immigration and border security, and he's now underwater on every issue we ask about," Morris said. "The president's policies have even harmed Republicans, with voters now more likely to say they trust Democrats to handle the issues of immigration and the economy."   Among adults, prices and inflation are collectively mentioned far and away as the most important problem facing the country today, with 63% of respondents saying it was one of their top three most important problems and 39% listing it first. Other top issues include jobs and the economy, health care, elections and democracy and immigration.   Taken all together, the sentiment of the electorate explains why Democrats and Republicans are spending big in House and Senate races stretching deep into conservative territory where Trump performed well in 2024.   
   Americans have soured on Trump and Republicans   Voters chose to give Republicans control of the White House and Congress in the 2024 election, and at least some of them say they regret their choice. According to the poll, nearly one in 10 people who said they voted in the 2024 presidential race regret their choice, including almost 15% of self-described Trump voters and 15% who backed a third-party candidate.   In May 2025, the Strength in Numbers/Verasight poll found voters trusted Republicans more than Democrats on immigration and deportations by an average of 15 points. Now, they trust Democrats by a narrow one point margin.   In every measure that the poll has tracked, Republicans have lost ground in the last year and a half, and only hold a slim advantage on crime and public safety issues and border security.   When asked which party voters trust to handle their personal top issue, Democrats hold a 47-35 advantage, a nearly 10-point jump since May 2025 and the widest gap measured.   
   The midterms are a referendum   Many polls, including the September NPR/PBS News/Marist survey, find that the 2026 midterm choices are best viewed in relation to Trump rather than a pure binary vote of support for the Democratic or Republican candidates.   Only 25% of respondents said it was more important to elect a Congress that will help Trump pass his agenda, compared to 58% who said it was about electing a Congress to act as a check and balance on Trump.   Two of every five voters surveyed said their decision would mostly be a statement against Trump and his agenda, compared to one in five who said it would be a statement of support. For 20% of voters surveyed, their choice would be about specific issues and candidates in their district.   On the issues of tariffs and trade, health care, foreign policy, elections and voting, government spending and social programs, immigration and deportations and artificial intelligence, a majority of those surveyed want a Congress to roll back or act as a check on Trump's stances.   
   More voters think the Democratic Party cares more about people like them than Republicans, and 20% say neither party does.

title: California gas prices have long plagued Democratic candidates. This year is different
description: Gas prices in California continue to be the highest in the nation, but the war in Iran has given California Democrats a rare opportunity to tur
body:
Gas prices in California continue to be the highest in the nation, but the war in Iran has given California Democrats a rare opportunity to turn the tables on the issue.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    JUANA SUMMERS, HOST:  In California, gas prices remain the highest in the nation. And pain at the pump has been a hot topic in the state's most competitive races for Congress. The issue has long favored California's Republicans. But the war in Iran has given Democrats a rare opening to turn the tables. From member station KQED, Guy Marzorati reports.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)MARNI VON WILPERT: No pain, no gain? Tell that to a family...GUY MARZORATI, BYLINE: In this ad, Marni von Wilpert is standing where few California Democrats have dared to go - a gas station.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)VON WILPERT: Not spend them on foreign wars that cost you money.MARZORATI: Democrats here have long been on the defensive over California's nation-high gas prices, driven by environmental rules that limit carbon emissions and a gas tax that pays for transportation, policies put in place by Democrats at the state capitol. But Democratic candidates like von Wilpert are pointing to the war in Iran for this year's prolonged increases.VON WILPERT: The first thing we saw with the closure of the Strait of Hormuz was the spike in gas prices.MARZORATI: Von Wilpert is running in the 48th House District, a southern California seat held by retiring Republican Congressman Darrell Issa. It's one of the most competitive in the state, according to the Cook Political Report. Von Wilpert is running here against Republican Jim Desmond and says, in this district...VON WILPERT: We need our cars. You know, it's a large district. There's not enough transit to get around without them, and so people are feeling the pain at the gas pump.MARZORATI: The 48th District is among the heaviest driving districts in California, according to a Brookings Institution analysis of annual vehicle miles traveled. Adie Tomer is a senior fellow at Brookings.ADIE TOMER: Across the country, districts that are represented by Republican-elected officials are disproportionately those districts where people drive longer distances.(SOUNDBITE OF TRAFFIC WHOOSHING)MARZORATI: Robin Ferguson lives in the district. She plans to vote for the Democrat, von Wilpert, in November.ROBIN FERGUSON: When we don't have the public transportation up here in North County to get down to San Diego that some of the other areas do, gas prices is a big issue.MARZORATI: And it's an issue that Democrats are increasingly talking about as they look to win back Congress. Nationally, over 60% of ads mentioning gas prices have come from Democrats, according to AdImpact, a complete reversal from 2024. But this is California, and Republicans are also campaigning on gas prices.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)KEVIN LINCOLN: Thanks to Adam Gray and Gavin Newsom, you get charged extra every time you fill up.UNIDENTIFIED ACTOR: Stupid California gas tax.MARZORATI: In another swing seat, Republican Kevin Lincoln is attacking Democratic incumbent Adam Gray for his vote to raise the state gas tax to fund road repair when he was in the state assembly.LINCOLN: And that's what makes California so different.MARZORATI: Christian Martinez is a spokesman for the National Republican Congressional Committee.CHRISTIAN MARTINEZ: There are specific votes, specific policies that voters can examine rather than simply looking at what's happening in Washington.MARZORATI: Back in the San Diego area, that argument is resonating with Gabriel Uribe, a construction worker who stopped to fill up his pickup truck in San Marcos. High gas prices were the top reason he voted for Donald Trump in 2024.GABRIEL URIBE: Oh, for sure. Yeah. It's No. 1, why, you know, I voted the way I did in the last presidential elections. It's just that it went - it still can't change unless we change here.MARZORATI: And until things change at the state level, Uribe says, the blame for high gas prices should stay with the Democrats.For NPR News, I'm Guy Marzorati in San Marcos, California.(SOUNDBITE OF LIL WAYNE AND ROBIN THICKE SONG, "SHOOTER")

title: Vivek Ramaswamy's attack ad features mother of Amy Acton, who alleges childhood abuse
description: A campaign ad by Republican candidate for Ohio governor Vivek Ramaswamy includes the mother of Democrat Amy Acton. Acton says they've been estr
body:
A campaign ad by Republican candidate for Ohio governor Vivek Ramaswamy includes the mother of Democrat Amy Acton. Acton says they've been estranged since she was abused as a child by her stepfather.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    SCOTT DETROW, HOST:  An attack ad from the campaign of Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican candidate for Ohio governor, has thrown that race into turmoil. And just to mention, in the coming story we are going to talk about sexual abuse. In the ad, the estranged mother of the Democratic candidate, Amy Acton, says her daughter is a liar. Acton has long talked about being sexually abused by her stepfather and how her mother stayed with him after his arrest. George Shillcock of WOSU Public Media in Columbus joins us now. Hey, there.GEORGE SHILLCOCK, BYLINE: Hello.DETROW: Let's start with the ad. What does it say?SHILLCOCK: In the ad, a woman named Donna Arthur urges people not to vote for her daughter.(SOUNDBITE OF AD)DONNA ARTHUR: She is a liar. She lies about her past.SHILLCOCK: She disputed a story Acton's told for years of her difficult childhood, where she and her younger brother were homeless at one point and lived in a tent with her mother and stepfather. At first, we didn't know who created the ad because the video didn't have the required disclosure that says who paid for it. But then, Tuesday, Ramaswamy told reporters it is an ad from his campaign. Here he is.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)VIVEK RAMASWAMY: I would love for this race, in this election, to be about the substantive issues that impact Ohioans. And unfortunately, Amy Acton has been hiding from those issues.DETROW: So WOSU had an interview with Acton yesterday just as all of this was breaking. What was her response?SHILLCOCK: Yes, our talk show All Sides with Amy Juravich was already scheduled to have Acton on. She explained how she and her mother have been estranged for over 50 years. Acton says her stepfather raped her. Court records produced by the campaign - and we verified - show they lived in a tent, and Arthur lost custody of Acton and her little brother. Acton's stepfather was charged but left the state with Arthur before he could be tried. He's deceased. Here's what Acton told us.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED NPR CONTENT)AMY ACTON: I was removed from her at the age of 12 - my brother was 9 - for child abuse and neglect that got bad enough we were actually living in a tent in the middle of winter.SHILLCOCK: Acton says it was awful to see her mother this way and criticized Ramaswamy for using Arthur in an ad like this.DETROW: Let's take a step back because here we are in late October talking about a close gubernatorial race in Ohio. This is a state that has not elected a Democratic governor in - what? - 20 years?SHILLCOCK: Yes, that's correct. The last Democratic governor was elected in 2006. And Trump has won the state three times. But the Cook Political Report rates this as a toss-up. On WOSU's talk show today, Bowling Green State University political science professor Robert Alexander says there is potential that the ad backfires on Ramaswamy. One issue during the campaign has been Acton's refusal to debate Ramaswamy. Alexander, who is on the state's debate commission and wants the debate to happen, is more understanding of her decision after seeing this ad.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED NPR CONTENT)ROBERT ALEXANDER: With all of that said, in the last 12 hours or so, one can understand why Amy Acton didn't want to have a debate. The kinds of things that can be said, you can't unsay those things.SHILLCOCK: Alexander says the story of Acton's childhood makes Acton seem resilient.DETROW: What should we be looking for in the final days of this race?SHILLCOCK: We'll see how this ad affects the race, but it's making others take sides. Today, Vice President Vance appeared at a rally in Ohio and defended the ad, saying Ramaswamy was right to run an ad that, quote, "calls Amy Acton a liar," unquote. But Republican former U.S. Ambassador Nikki Haley posted on X that Ramaswamy is a, quote, "bad guy." She ran against him in the presidential primary in 2024. Libertarian candidate for governor Don Kissick called on Ramaswamy to drop out. Meanwhile, Trump and former President Barack Obama plan to come here to campaign for their party's candidates in the coming week.DETROW: That is George Shillcock of WOSU in Columbus, Ohio. Thank you so much.SHILLCOCK: Thank you.

title: Supreme Court upholds pause on Trump's anti-trans prison policy
description: A view of the U.S. Supreme Court in Wash
body:
A view of the U.S. Supreme Court in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 14.
                
                    Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   The Supreme Court ruled Wednesday that the Trump administration must continue providing gender-affirming care to transgender inmates in federal prisons.   The decision, in an emergency appeal, maintains a lower court's injunction on a federal Bureau of Prisons' policy that would terminate hormone therapy and other treatments for trans inmates.   The unsigned order offered no explanation behind the decision. It simply read, "The application for stay presented to The Chief Justice and by him referred to the Court is denied."   It also said Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito would side with the Trump administration and would grant the application for stay.   
   As the federal judge's injunction remains in place, the legal battle over the policy continues.   In January 2025, upon assuming office, Trump issued an executive order banning the use of federal funds that "promote" gender ideology. And prisoners brought a class action seeking reinstatement of the decades-long health policy. It contends that the Trump policy violates the Eighth Amendment's ban on cruel and unusual punishment.   A federal district judge barred the BOP from implementing its policy this summer.   A second court, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, also rejected the administration's request to pause U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth's order.   That's when U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer asked the Supreme Court to intervene.   As the federal judge's injunction remains in place, the legal battle over the policy continues.   Li Nowlin-Sohl, senior staff attorney at the American Civil Liberties Union and a lawyer involved in this case, said the organization believes there are more than 2,000 people in BOP custody who identify as transgender. (The BOP stopped publishing data reflecting transgender inmates after Trump took office in 2025. It only records male or female individuals incarcerated in the federal system.)   Kingdom v. Trump represents 1,000 inmates who have a gender dysphoria diagnosis, Nowlin-Sohl explained. Of those, the ACLU believes there are about 800 who have been prescribed hormone therapy and many who are also receiving social transition accommodations, Nowlin-Sohl said.   
   In its request for an emergency stay on the earlier rulings, the Trump administration argued that providing this care poses several risks, including for recipients of this specialized care, who it argued would become "targets for attacks." They also said that it raises "fairness concerns" as it would "breed resentment" with other inmates.   Access to gender-affirming care is considered medically necessary to treat gender dysphoria, a medical term used to describe the deep discomfort caused by a mismatch between a person's assigned sex at birth and their gender identity. Without it, individuals can struggle severely with mental health issues such as heightened anxiety and depression, with some turning to self-harm and suicide.   Gender-affirming care can include "...hormone therapy, and gender-affirming surgeries among others," according to the World Professional Association for Transgender Health. (In its filings, the Trump administration questioned WPATH's standards of care, which were developed by experts in transgender health and used by organizations across the world.)   Some people who are transgender may require hormone therapy and gender-affirming surgeries; others may not require any of these interventions.   The BOP has treated people diagnosed with gender dysphoria since at least 1992, the ACLU said in response to the government's filings to the Supreme Court.   "Had BOP's doctors found this treatment unhelpful or harmful to patients or had the agency found that the treatment compromised security, surely BOP would have mentioned it in the administrative record," the ACLU wrote.   This is a "glaring omission" and appears to indicate that the government's arguments now are simply "contrived," the ACLU continued.   NPR previously covered the impact of the loss of hormone treatments on people who are incarcerated. One woman said she experienced severe physical and mental anguish when she lost access to hormone treatments.   The Supreme Court's decision is at odds with other rulings that support the Trump administration's anti-trans policy agenda.   
   Last June, the court ruled that states can ban transgender girls from participating in sports at publicly funded schools. And in 2025, the court upheld state laws that make it illegal for doctors and other health professionals to provide gender-affirming care for minors.   In one of his first executive orders of his second term, President Trump targeted the trans community with a declaration that his administration recognizes just two sexes, male and female. This order has been the basis for a host of anti-trans policies throughout the administration.   But at least for now, the emergency request on the prison policy was to no avail.   Waiting in the wings at the Supreme Court are other cases on transgender rights. Most prominently, the Alliance Defending Freedom, an anti-trans group, has filed an emergency petition at the court on behalf of a mother and her teenage daughter who contend that the daughter was "unknowingly" forced to face a transgender opponent in girl's high school wrestling. Later this year, the court will hear oral arguments in a case testing whether a religious preschool can receive state funding while excluding LGBTQ families. In a separate case, the justices will examine whether parents have the right to challenge a state law that allows runaway teens to receive gender-affirming care without parental consent.   NPR Legal Affairs Correspondent Nina Totenberg contributed reporting.

title: Trump leans into unprecedented power ahead of midterm elections
description: President Trump boards Air Force One on
body:
President Trump boards Air Force One on Oct. 19 at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland.
                
                    Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
    

   
   President Trump boasted this weekend of his growing power in his second term — and all the things he's doing now that he wouldn't dare in his first term, such as changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America.   "I don't think I could have done this in my first term," he told supporters in Northern Kentucky, "This is a much more powerful term. I can do stuff that's unbelievable."   He joked about how big companies wouldn't take his call in the first term, but "now they kiss my ass."   Less than two weeks before the election, Trump continues to crash through barriers that he wouldn't dare cross in his first term — and pointing to that power to make his case to midterm voters.   
   Trump's Justice Department is raiding a congresswoman's home. He's knocking down trees in Washington, D.C., against a judge's wishes. And he's making deals with Russia that fly in the face of congressionally passed sanctions.   Trump is hardly the first president to become frustrated and test the limits of executive authority.   George W. Bush issued controversial "signing statements" to challenge or reinterpret bills passed by Congress. Barack Obama famously said he had a pen and he planned to use it. Trump is part of that trend.   Trump inherited an increasingly powerful presidency, said Tevi Troy, a presidential historian who worked in the George W. Bush White House.   Congress has been basically giving away its own power for a quarter of a century. And Troy says Trump is using that power in a distinctive way — and not to just get around congressional gridlock.   Trump's using it to also go after political and cultural opponents.   "His goals include going after some of his opponents reining in 'woke' or 'DEI' stuff at universities, pushing back against the media," Troy said, adding: "He's what I call a unilateralist. He doesn't have an ideology, he has a methodology, and the methodology is unilateralism."   The targets are not entirely surprising. Trump has spent years attacking news organizations, criticizing regulators, and confronting political opponents, including members of his own party.   
   Ryan Williams, a Republican strategist who helped lead Mitt Romney's presidential campaign, described Trump as a brawler who won't hesitate to use those extraordinary powers in all those fights.   "Trump has made it very clear that he wants to approach his second term in a way where he gets what he wants," Williams said. "He's the president, he's the boss, and he's not going to be restrained by traditions or aides that may say you should hold back."   The question is no longer how much Trump can accomplish through executive action. It's how far the president can go and what, if anything, will constrain him.   In another example, the Trump administration announced earlier this month investigations against nine universities, including Harvard and Yale, for allegedly bringing in international students in order to undercut American wages.   If the administration doesn't like a person or organization's point of view, Trump officials are "prepared to take the gloves off," said Frank Sesno, a former CNN Washington bureau chief who is now a media and public affairs professor at George Washington University.   Sesno said that could be waged in court or through contracts, revoking security clearances or launching investigations.   "These are the extensions of power that can only be exercised in many ways by the executive branch of the federal government," Sesno said. "And they are awesome weapons."

title: Top 2 Democrats on Intel say they're preparing for Trump to claim foreign meddling
description: President Trump walks to board Air Force
body:
President Trump walks to board Air Force One on Oct. 20 at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland.
                
                    Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
    

   
   The top Democrats on the House and Senate intelligence committees say they are operating under the presumption that President Trump and his allies will allege fraud related to this year's midterms in order to justify election interference.   "We start with the premise that the president is going to do that. It would be irresponsible not to, speaking as somebody who was in the chamber on January 6, 2021," said Rep. Jim Himes, D-Conn. "We're making the assumption that the president is not going to accept the results of what looks to be a very challenging election for him and his party."   
   Speaking alongside Himes on Wednesday, Mark Warner of Virginia, the top Democrat on the Senate Intelligence Committee, said that one way the president could do that: claiming foreign interference in the voting process.   "President Trump has done more than any other President to ensure we have free and fair elections," said White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis in a statement to NPR. "While extreme Democrats and the media continue to dismiss concerns about voter fraud, the Trump Administration is taking decisive action to protect our elections including prosecuting election crimes, strengthening election infrastructure security, and protecting vulnerable voters from fraud and coercion."   Asked if he would accept the results of the election by a reporter earlier this month, Trump replied, "What do you think? Of course I will, but we don't want cheating."   
   Himes and Warner are members of the Gang of Eight, senior lawmakers who oversee the nation's spy agencies and receive confidential briefings.   In a briefing for reporters, Warner and Himes said they have made clear to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and other intelligence leaders that they must be immediately reachable by phone on and after Election Day in the event that Trump alleges foreign interference in the election. Or, Himes said, if the president "decides to use allegations of foreign interference as an excuse to seize ballot boxes, question the validity of the election."   
   "If, at noon on Election Day, the president announced that the Iranians have undertaken operation," Himes said, "I'm on TV saying 'I'm Gang of Eight and I have received no such briefing, no such information, and I have no reason to believe that this is accurate.'"   "Now, does that end the crisis? No, but that's the first step," Himes said.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Rep. Jim Himes, D-Conn., speaks during a House Select Intelligence Committee hearing on March 19, 2026. Himes says he expects President Trump to allege fraud in this year's midterms in order to justify election interference.
                
                    Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
    

   
   Both lawmakers said that they are in close contact with top Trump intelligence officials, even as they allege that those leaders have failed to provide legally mandated pre-election reports to Congress assessing the state of play regarding foreign election meddling efforts.   "When Jay Clayton assumed his role as DNI, we asked and received the required classified summary of influence and interference," Himes said. "We have not received a bunch of things that we have asked for," including, he said the statutorily required reports about the state of play 120 days, 60 days and 30 days before the election.   The ODNI office did not immediately reply to a request for comment.   The lawmakers said that they had received one classified report on Tuesday from the DNI's office, which detailed what they described as a "grabbag" of intelligence on meddling efforts, including the sort of Russian and Chinese campaigns that have come to be expected in American elections.   "The state of play, I would argue, is Russia, similar to prior occasions, is going after Democrats, usually with misinformation," Warner said. "Iran is probably more looking at disruption in Europe. They've been more anti-Trump. China's been more selective, oftentimes on local races or smaller issues, oftentimes with Chinese nationals involved."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Jay Clayton, left, shakes hands with Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., following his confirmation hearing for Director of National Intelligence on July 15, 2026. Warner says administration officials have failed to provide legally mandated pre-election reports to Congress on foreign election meddling efforts.
                
                    Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images
    

   
   Still, Himes said that there is a "profound distinction" between those influence campaigns and actual interference in election infrastructure itself, "which is messing around with the voting rolls, with the machines … which is very, very difficult."   
   Himes specifically emphasized that "we have never seen an operation to actually interfere and, as of now, we are not seeing either the capability or the intent to interfere."   Their preparations for a possible fraudulent claim of foreign interference is one part of a much larger election integrity effort by the Democrats and good governance groups.   "There is a plan there," Warner said, noting that a constellation of more than 75 groups are still meeting on a regular basis, "fully lawyered up." But he suggested that the responsibility to protect democracy is much broader than good governance groups and lawmakers themselves, and extends to the press and the public at large.   
   "I think any potential mishap, from seating of members of Congress to the count after the fact, I know both of us have spent time with former military members, intel members, business leaders, civil society to make the case that if something happens, you have to speak up," Warner said.   Asked if he thought Republican lawmakers would speak out, the senator replied that hope springs eternal.   "I think everybody realizes what's at stake here. I mean, the irony of celebrating our 250th anniversary and this the first year we had a completely corrupt election?" Warner said. "I think people know what's at stake."   Do you have information about midterm election influence or protection efforts you would like to share? Reach out to Eric McDaniel on Signal at ericmcdaniel.92

title: The Justice Department begins notifying counties where it wants to monitor elections
description: People walk by a polling place at Denver
body:
People walk by a polling place at Denver's Central Library on June 30, 2026.
                
                    Michael Ciaglo/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Michael Ciaglo/Getty Images
    

   
   The Department of Justice this week began notifying the counties it wants to monitor on Election Day, NPR has learned.   Counties in Colorado, Florida, Minnesota, Texas and Washington have received notifications from the Justice Department so far, but the list seems to be growing in real time.   The department has long deployed monitors to ensure compliance with voting laws, but the Trump administration's unprecedented steps to try to wrestle control over elections from local and state governments have led to new concerns about DOJ monitoring this year. And already this week, at least one county official is raising questions about why his locality is on the DOJ's list.   
   Last month, Harmeet Dhillon, the head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, said the department planned to send 1,000 observers nationwide, in what she termed "the largest monitoring effort" in DOJ history.   
   And even as counties are being notified, it's unclear which jurisdictions or how many the department plans to monitor this November. A DOJ spokesperson, Kiersten Pels, told NPR those details will be shared "closer to the election."   The Justice Department routinely observes elections. The department under President Biden monitored 64 jurisdictions in 24 states on Election Day in the last midterm year, 2022.   But to many local officials and experts, this year is different.   President Trump continues to falsely maintain that he won the 2020 election and that election fraud is more widespread than it has ever been proven to be. Experts worry federal law enforcement could potentially use those false claims — or others generated this year — as pretext to try to seize ballots during the counting period, or interfere in the process in some other way.   Most states reported no incidents with Justice Department monitors during primary elections earlier this year, but in Wyoming, the state's Republican governor expressed concern about "aggressive" and "irregular" behavior by monitors for the state's August primary. And the Republican county clerk of Laramie County told NBC News that the conduct of the monitors "showed complete disregard for our state laws and administration of our elections."   
   The Department of Justice disputes that characterization.   "We disagree with the public framing that the two monitors we sent were 'aggressive' or did anything improper," Pels said, adding that Dhillon had a meeting with the Wyoming officials after the fact.   In previous election cycles, state officials in the states where monitors were assigned were notified at the same time as the counties. This year, that did not happen initially, according to officials in three states who spoke to NPR anonymously because they weren't authorized to speak to the press. So states have been scrambling since the notifications began going out Tuesday to figure out where the DOJ plans to be.   After NPR asked the DOJ why states had not been notified, multiple state officials told NPR they then received notification from the department.   
   One of the counties that received a notification is Adams County, Colo.   The clerk there, Democrat Josh Zygielbaum, told NPR he wasn't shocked the DOJ selected his county to observe, as Adams County includes part of the state's 8th Congressional District, a toss-up district that could determine party control of the House of Representatives next year.   Zygielbaum was surprised however that the DOJ reached out only to him, and not the Republican clerk in neighboring Weld County, which also houses a sizable portion of that same congressional district.   "My initial thought is that it's politically motivated, and that this is potentially an intimidation technique," Zygielbaum said. "Although I like to assume the best in people, the administration really has shown its disdain for elections, particularly in states and counties where mail ballots exist."   Pels, of the DOJ, said the department prioritizes places with competitive elections, and would monitor Adams County because it is covered by Section 203 of the Voting Rights Act, which requires voters be given access to election materials in the language they speak. Weld County is not covered under that provision.   
   That explanation didn't fully comfort Zygielbaum.   "The fact that we're covered by Section 203 means we have a higher portion of Spanish-speaking voters who have a right to vote," Zygielbaum said. "It still doesn't put me at ease that it's not a targeted visit."   
   NPR reported in September that Trump administration officials assigned to noncitizen voting issues last year circulated a list of counties covered by Section 203, along with a DOJ criminal checklist outlining requirements for prosecution of voter-related charges.   Colorado state officials say they are considering how to respond to the DOJ's request, considering Colorado election rules say observers need to have permission from the secretary of state's office, unless they are ordered to observe by a court.   "We are considering these requests in collaboration with the Attorney General's Office," said Jack Todd, a spokesperson for the Colorado secretary of state's office.   Zygielbaum says his election processes won't change either way. He has, however, already requested a staffer from the state come to Adams County on Election Day just to keep an eye on the federal monitors if they do come.   "I have lots of questions about why they're there and what their ultimate intent is," he said.   NPR has confirmed the DOJ has also sent monitor notifications to seven counties in Texas, King County, Wash., Miami-Dade County, Fla., and Hennepin and Ramsey counties in Minnesota.   The DOJ requested to send monitors to the same Minnesota counties during the state's primary in August, but monitors were denied close access to polling locations. A spokesperson for the Minnesota secretary of state's office said it was too soon to know whether a different decision would be made for this fall's general election.   In 2024, Texas similarly blocked the Biden-era DOJ from election monitoring. Ken Paxton, the state attorney general and current Republican nominee for U.S. Senate, went to court then to block monitors from getting inside polling and counting locations.   
   "The DOJ knows it has no authority to monitor Texas elections and backed down when Texas stood up for the rule of law," Paxton said in a statement on Nov. 5, 2024.

schema.headline: The Justice Department begins notifying counties where it wants to monitor elections

title: How Trump's attacks on voting system integrity might affect upcoming elections
description:
Transcript
        
    DAVE DAVIES, HOST:  This is FRESH AIR. I'm Dave Davies. The midterm election is less than two weeks a
body:
Transcript
        
    DAVE DAVIES, HOST:  This is FRESH AIR. I'm Dave Davies. The midterm election is less than two weeks away. And for months, President Donald Trump has been warning that American voting systems are not to be trusted, including in his July primetime address to the nation.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: Hundreds of thousands of noncitizens and dead people are listed and active on the voter rolls. And yet we still have elections with no voter ID, no proof of citizenship and tens of millions of ballots flowing aimlessly through the mail.DAVIES: Trump has claimed that mail-in ballots may be forged, that voting machines can be hacked and that corrupt Democrats will conspire to steal votes, as he claims they did in his 2020 loss to Joe Biden. He's tried to affect the election by imposing new restrictions on registration and voting, requiring the Post Office to screen who can receive mail-in ballots and demanding that states purge thousands of people from voter rolls. Those moves have mostly been blocked by courts, but many election experts worry that Trump's claims are laying the basis to challenge the outcome of the midterms if results don't go his way.Today, we're going to speak to two experts on elections. A little later, we'll talk to Al Schmidt, the chief elections official in the swing state of Pennsylvania. But first, we'll speak to Richard Hasen. He's director of the Safeguarding Democracy Project at the UCLA Law School and founder of the popular Election Law Blog. He's author of the book "A Real Right To Vote: How A Constitutional Amendment Can Safeguard American Democracy," now in paperback, and a forthcoming book, "Unbent Arc: The Rise And Decline Of American Democracy 1964-2024." We recorded our conversation yesterday.Well, Rick Hasen, welcome back to FRESH AIR.RICK HASEN: It's good to be with you.DAVIES: You know, you've written that several attempts by President Trump to interfere with the coming election have been decisively defeated. One of them was an effort mostly by the Department of Homeland Security to get states to purge large numbers of people from their voting rolls - people the administration said they had identified as likely noncitizens registered to vote. That effort, it turns out, is still active, at least in California. But first, tell us what we know about where these lists of noncitizen voters came from.HASEN: So the United States is pretty unique compared to other advanced democracies in that we don't have a national identity card. We don't have a national database of all of our voters. We don't automatically register our voters. So we face problems here in terms of knowing who is eligible to vote and, when they move from place to place, to change their voter registration.So the federal government has some data on citizenship. It's got something called the SAVE database. We know that this database is not all that reliable. We also know that it's not all that up to date. So sometimes it might flag someone as a noncitizen who in recent months might have been naturalized as a citizen. And so the federal government has been using the SAVE database, as well as some other commercially available databases, to try to come up with a list of citizens that they're trying to have the states compare with their own state voter registration lists to take out people who are not eligible to be voting.DAVIES: Right. And we should note that it's been reported that the Department of Homeland Security has had hundreds of agents scouring these various state voter lists to try and find these allegedly noncitizen registered voters, right?HASEN: Yes. So they've been doing that. One of the problems is that there are many people with the same names. And unless you have really good, identifiable information like Social Security numbers and driver's license numbers, it's possible to make mistakes. So that's one of the reasons why the federal government has sued to try to get what are called the unredacted lists that have all of that personal information.Most states - it's against the law to provide that information to anyone. And the federal government sued 31 states and Washington D.C. And so far, they're zero for 26 in their lawsuits to try to get these unredacted voting rolls. And that's in part because our Constitution doesn't give the federal government the power to run elections. It says that states run elections. Congress can pass statutes that govern some of the aspects of congressional elections, but there's no role for the federal government. And so here you have the Trump administration trying to intrude on what's traditionally been a state and local prerogative.DAVIES: So in some cases, the federal government - the Department of Homeland Security - has given states actual lists of people and said, look at these people. You should purge them. How have states responded to that?HASEN: Well, Nevada is a good example. So a few months ago, the Department of Homeland Security said they had identified hundreds of thousands of noncitizens across four different states. One of them was Nevada. There were 16,000 people on this possible list. It got whittled down to 185. And eventually, when state officials investigated, it went down to zero. That is, all of the 16,000 people who were identified either were not registered to vote or were eligible to register to vote.In California, in that same report, the Department of Homeland Security, without providing the data, said that there were up to 190,000 noncitizens. Now, in the most recent actions in California, they've whittled that number down to 20,000. And so far, they've arrested 28. And it appears from those arrests that at least some of those people either were not registered to vote or did not break the law intentionally.DAVIES: Right. And as I understand it, this list of 20,000 names that they wanted the state of California and officials in Los Angeles to check was simply provided to them on a thumb drive with a password on a sticky note? Is that right?HASEN: Yeah. So it's worth taking a step back and recognizing how unusual this whole set of events is. So ordinarily, there's a lot of cooperation between the federal government and state and local governments in terms of administering elections. Now we have this very different situation where the states and localities are seeing the federal government as kind of an adversary that's been threatening state and local election officials with prosecution if they don't adequately police their voting rolls in ways that the Trump administration wants.And the idea that in the middle of an election - you know, in California, ballots are already out. We're getting into the period of in-person early voting - that in this period that the federal government would send on a thumb drive, with the password on a sticky note, the names of 20,000 possible noncitizen voters and ask 48 hours for the state to agree to go through this list and purge voters - I mean, it's just incredible. It's not the kind of thing that ever has happened that I'm aware of.And there's a federal law called the National Voter Registration Act. It's a law that was passed when Bill Clinton was president in 1993. And it says that states can't do these last-minute voter purges because doing so risks disenfranchising eligible voters.DAVIES: Now, as you said, 28 people were charged with either having registered or voted as noncitizens earlier this week. Some were actually arrested and taken to court. Just tell us what that experience was like, as it's been reported.HASEN: Well, it seems clear that this was a publicity stunt that was meant to back up the federal government's attempt to get an order from a judge - a temporary restraining order that would require California to go through this list and segregate out ballots from people who are on this list. So we know that a branch of the Department of Homeland Security did a 5 a.m. raid. There were helicopters, SWAT team to arrest a man in pretty bad health. He had recently had six surgeries. He was arrested and taken into custody. And eventually, four hours later, they told him what he was charged with. He has no idea what's going on here.What we know from what the Los Angeles Times has reported is that many of these people don't even know why they were arrested. And in the case of the man who was taken in the predawn raid, it's possible that a relative who has the same name, who is a U.S. citizen, was confused for this person who was arrested, and it may be that it is the person who is allowed to vote, whose name is on the voter list rather than the person who was arrested.DAVIES: And I believe it was reported that the four people who on the first day made their first appearance in court often appeared in, like, shackles - right? - leg irons in some cases, and then were released on their own recognizance.HASEN: Yes. And the federal government tipped off the New York Post, which was given an exclusive to cover this. There were photographers from the Associated Press. This was clearly an orchestrated effort to make it appear that noncitizen voting is a huge problem. The headline at the New York Post talked about a network of people conspiring to commit fraud. But there's no conspiracy charge. There's no evidence that any of the people who were charged even know each other. So this really seems to be a show, which might be for various reasons, but it doesn't seem to be for legitimate law enforcement purposes.DAVIES: And we should note that in many states, there have been cases where voters, when they got driver's license, as many immigrants have, were registered to vote, in some cases, without their knowledge, or at least it wasn't exactly clear that they understood they were being registered, right?HASEN: Yes. So this takes a little bit of explanation. So the 1993 law the National Voter Registration Act, among other things, provides that state offices like Departments of Motor Vehicles, have to offer opportunities for people who get their driver's license or do business at the DMV to register to vote. When you are at the DMV and you are presented with the opportunity to register to vote, you're asked if you're a citizen. And sometimes you're asked on one of those PIN pads, which I know - at least here in California, they're sometimes hard to read. It's possible that someone mischecks a box, and they inadvertently get registered to vote.We had a situation recently in New Jersey where because of an error by a vendor of software that the Department of Motor Vehicles there used, there were 6,000 noncitizens who were inadvertently registered to vote. Those people were sent registration materials. They were sent voting materials. We know that 400 of them voted. But that doesn't necessarily prove any criminal intent. In order to be criminally liable for violating the federal law against noncitizen voting, the federal government has to prove that you willfully violated the law.Those votes, of course, are illegal, and they need to be removed from the voting rolls. But in terms of finding a large criminal conspiracy or, you know, some kind of effort to register noncitizens and get them to vote in a particular way, we just haven't seen that. The last credible allegations of something like this go back to the 1980s in California.DAVIES: Another effort that you note President Trump made was to get the Post Office involved in the distribution of absentee ballots. What did he do? How did that turn out?HASEN: So President Trump has issued two executive orders on elections. So in the first executive order, he tried to get a federal agency called the United States Election Assistance Commission to change the form that the federal government has for people to register to vote to require people to provide documentary proof of citizenship, like a birth certificate or a naturalization certificate, before they can register to vote. That effort was stopped by courts, which said that the president has no role to play in the conduct of elections. That didn't deter the president. He issued a second executive order in March of this year, and among other things, it created a whole system for the United States Postal Service to become the arbiters of which mail-in ballots they would accept from states. And it was very convoluted process.First, it required the states to provide certain ballot envelope designs, and those had to be approved by the United States Postal Service. Then each envelope had to contain a unique machine-readable barcode so that each individual envelope could be tracked to know who it's going to. And then the state would have to upload a list of their voters. And the Postal Service would have to match the envelopes that are submitted by the state with the list of voters, and it would have to reject an entire batch of these ballots if there was any discrepancy between the list and what was on the ballots.This was a very complicated system, but what made it particularly troublesome in this election is that the Postal Service hadn't gotten its act together. It had not set up the web portal that its own rules said it was going to set up for the states to upload their citizenship to the database. And what this would have meant is that the United States Postal Service would not have been allowed to accept even a single ballot from any state because no state would be able to upload its list of citizens. It took three trips to the Supreme Court to stop the United States Postal Service from putting into effect a rule that would have shut down mail-in balloting for the 2026 elections. Now, this rule is still in litigation, and there's a chance that it will be in effect for the 2028 elections. The court orders only involve the 2026 elections. But by 2028, presumably, at least the USPS will have a working portal so that states that want to comply would be able to.DAVIES: Richard Hasen directs the Safeguarding Democracy Project at the UCLA Law School. We'll continue our conversation after a break. This is FRESH AIR.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)DAVIES: This is FRESH AIR, and we're speaking with Richard Hasen, director of the Safeguarding Democracy Project at the UCLA Law School and founder of the Election Law Blog. Let's talk about some other efforts that might be made by the president in the course of the midterms. One thing that's been written about is that he could declare a national emergency and thereby mobilize federal resources to intervene directly in voting. What about that prospect?HASEN: Well, the president's already declared a national emergency at the southern border. When the president declares a national emergency, it unlocks certain powers for the president. But none of those powers are involving elections. So even if Trump declares a national emergency by falsely claiming, for example, that a foreign government is trying to interfere with U.S. elections, that still doesn't give the president the power over the administration of elections. If Donald Trump declared tomorrow that we're not going to hold elections, that would have no legal effect because it's not the federal government that runs elections. It's the states and the local governments.And Trump was on a right-wing podcast. He was asked about this. And he just said something like, stranger things have happened. So, you know, kind of keeping the conspiratorial right satisfied that he's considering this, but I think it's extremely unlikely he would do it. And if he did, I don't think it would have any effect on how our elections are actually run.DAVIES: Another fear is that armed law enforcement personnel will appear at polling places - like, particularly ICE agents. Can that happen?HASEN: I believe there are three different federal laws that bar armed federal officers from appearing at polling places. So it would be illegal, and if it happened, I think it would be possible to get a court order against it happening.But I think there's a more fundamental reason why I don't think it's going to happen. Remember, we're talking about a series of congressional elections and elections for Senate as well as for state and local offices. This is not like a presidential election where there's a battleground state, like we could say it all comes down to what happens in Pennsylvania or Wisconsin. There might be a very close election for Congress in Ohio or in California. There aren't enough ICE agents to send around.And also, we saw the reaction of the public in Minneapolis when there were these surges of ICE agents to try to engage in immigration activities. I think it would be a big risk of a political backlash against the president if there was an attempt to try to physically stop people from voting or to intimidate voters by sending ICE agents to the polls.DAVIES: Then there's the more extreme step of seizing ballots or voting machines. And I don't - this has never happened, and I - as far as I know - in an ongoing vote, right?HASEN: I think if the president is going to try to interfere with the elections, he's much more likely to do so on the back end of the election rather than the front end. By the front end, I mean when people are actually going and voting, millions of people going to polling places. It'd be very hard to disrupt that. It would be very public.What I'm more worried about in the event of a very close election for control of the House or Senate is that Trump's Department of Justice might try to interfere with the tabulation process - that's the counting of ballots - or the certification process, when state officials say, yeah, here's who the official winners are. And one way that the Department of Justice could potentially get involved is by trying to get a federal court order to seize ballots or seize voting machines. The reason we care about this is because Donald Trump has said that he regrets not seizing voting machines after the 2020 election that he lost to Joe Biden and contested.Now, we did have a seizure of ballots in 2025 in Fulton County, Georgia, that took the ballots from the 2020 election, so a long-completed election. We also had Tulsi Gabbard, the former director of national intelligence, have the Department of Homeland Security seize voting machines in Puerto Rico that were then taken and looked at by federal government workers. But what we have not had is the seizure of ballots or a voting machine in a live election - one where the winner has not yet been determined.When ballots or machines are taken out of the possession of election officials, you break what's called the electoral chain of custody. That is, one of the ways that we know that elections are free and fair is that the ballots are always under the control of election officials, and typically with transparency measures like cameras or other ways of observing, to make sure that no one is meddling with the ballots. If ballots are taken out of the custody of election officials, ballots could be added to or altered or taken away. It would be incredibly dangerous. It would require getting a search warrant from a federal judge.And so one of the things that we've been doing at the Safeguarding Democracy Project, and others have been working on, is trying to educate judges. Judges know a lot about criminal law. They know a lot about search warrants. They don't know a lot about how elections are run. And so we're trying to explain the kind of irreparable harm that can happen if ballots are allowed to be taken outside the custody of election officials. There are ways to satisfy legitimate law enforcement purposes if there is, in fact, probable cause that a crime has been committed. There are ways to protect those ballots as evidence without breaking the electoral chain of custody.DAVIES: We're going to take another break here. Let me reintroduce you. Richard Hasen is director of the Safeguarding Democracy Project at the UCLA Law School and founder of the Election Law Blog. He'll be back after this short break. I'm Dave Davies, and this is FRESH AIR.(SOUNDBITE OF BILL FRISELL'S "WASHINGTON POST MARCH")DAVIES: This is FRESH AIR. I'm Dave Davies. And we're talking about the potential effect of President Trump's repeated warnings of fraud in the midterm election, less than two weeks away. While Trump's attempts to impose restrictions on registration and voting have largely failed in the courts, some election experts worry that his claims are designed to lay the basis for challenging the outcome of the November 3 voting if things don't go his way. We're speaking with Richard Hasen, director of the Safeguarding Democracy Project at the UCLA Law School and founder of the popular Election Law Blog.The other prospect that people are talking about is that after the election, that the clerk of the United States House of Representatives, who was appointed by the speaker, Mike Johnson, could refuse to seat Democrats in closely contested races. What's the check on that?HASEN: Well - so to begin with, there's a political check. If, for example, the news organizations have said that Democrats have won enough elections to retake control of Congress - if the clerk, who is a bureaucrat, came in and said, well, no. These races are contested. We're not going to let these people be seated and get to vote for speaker of the House - I think that would be politically very dangerous. That would look like a literal coup d'etat. That is, it would be trying to turn an election loser into an election winner, in this case, through fraud.If it did happen, which I think is very unlikely, I think there would be resort to the courts. And courts would come in. Now, ordinarily, a court wouldn't interfere with a congressional process. The - under the separation of powers, that would be a political question. But the clerk who works for the House is not the House. And so I think the courts could hear such a challenge. And it's extremely unlikely that, both politically and legally, this kind of move could happen if, in fact, the Democrats have easily taken control of the House.Now, that leads me to a more general point about what we expect after November 3. It's all about the margins. If, in fact, we do not have a close election for control of the House or the Senate, I would be very surprised to see any attempts to try to wholesale change the results of the elections so that control of the House or Senate could flip.If the elections are very close - for example, suppose that control of the Senate comes down to who wins in Alaska - Alaska, which takes a very long time to count their ballots because of their rural populations and where they use ranked-choice voting, which takes longer to tabulate results. If it comes down to one seat, then I think all bets are off. And then I'm very concerned that the Trump administration will try to do things to manipulate the outcome of the elections.DAVIES: I know you've written about campaign finance. And the spending in this election is truly unprecedented by individuals. We've seen reporting that Elon Musk has pumped 276 million into the midterms, a figure that's probably out of date by now. Over 150 million has gone through a couple of transactions into the Texas state Senate race. What's this doing to our democracy? And what can we do about it?HASEN: So there's been a real sea change since the United States Supreme Court decided the Citizens United case in 2010. Some of it is legal change - the creation of super PACs. But even the seeds for super PACs, which are independent groups that can raise unlimited sums from individuals, corporations and unions - even the seeds for that were planted in a 1976 case called Buckley v. Valeo. But something has changed psychologically on the part of big donors in that they're no longer shy about putting their money into elections.And so just to give you some statistics, the first donor who gave at least $100 million to groups in a federal election was Sheldon Adelson back in 2018. We only had one or two people or couples in this category. A hundred million dollars - just an obscene amount of money for one person to be able to give an election.By the 2024 elections, we had nine individuals and couples who fit into that category. And Elon Musk set the record with almost $300 million in spending. I think he's likely to exceed that in a midterm election, which is even more astounding, when typically the spending is much lower than in a presidential election year. It's a fundamentally unfair system in which we allow the wealthiest of Americans to have outsized influence not only over who's elected by increasing the chances that the candidate they support will be elected thanks to all of the campaign dollars, but also outsized influence over what elected officials are going to do once they're in office.So if you are the recipient of Elon Musk's generosity, you're going to be very solicitous of his interests and what he wants to do. And if you're on the other side, you might fear doing something that might antagonize Elon Musk for fear that he could unleash really astronomical sums against you. And so the system - we might call it corruption. It certainly is an unequal system where the wealthiest among us are able to translate their economic power into political power.DAVIES: And what's the prospect for doing something about it?HASEN: The prospects for doing something about it in the short term are quite low because the current regime we have is the product of Supreme Court decisions, especially over the last 20 years. We have a very conservative Supreme Court that, on campaign finance issues, takes a very libertarian view of the First Amendment and sees most limits on money and politics as unconstitutional - as a violation of the rights of free speech and association.So how could you change that? You either have to change the Constitution or you have to change the Supreme Court. Both of those things are very difficult to do. Actually, I think it would be probably easier to change the Supreme Court than to get through a constitutional amendment, which requires supermajorities in both the House and Senate and supermajority of states to approve a constitutional amendment.So I think there's going to be a lot of pressure if Democrats retake the House and the Senate and the presidency in 2029 to try to deal with some of the issues related to our democracy, from campaign finance to partisan gerrymandering to the Supreme Court's evisceration of the Voting Rights Act.DAVIES: Well, briefly returning to the election in front of us, you know, The Washington Post recently reported that a group of former national security officials are warning state election officials to be on the lookout for meddling and interference on November 3. I'm wondering what you're going to be doing that day and how you anticipate affecting this - following it, covering it.HASEN: Usually Election Day is pretty quiet for me because things generally go smoothly. Of course, there's going to be someplace where there's a power outage and machines are not working, or a county didn't provide enough ballots to a polling place. There might be some last-minute skirmishing about whether polls need to be kept open an extra hour or two for people who were not able to vote. But it should be quiet on Election Day, especially because I think many people have been heeding the advice of election experts to vote early if you can. And I would say, if you're going to vote by mail, vote as early as possible or put that ballot in a dropbox or bring it to a voting center if that's allowed in your state. So hopefully it will be quiet.It'll be the day after Election Day or a couple of days after Election Day when we'll really have a sense of whether or not we're going to make it through this period. And in 2020, I warned that we would have a real danger of an attempt to interfere with free and fair elections - a peaceful transition of power. And people said that I was too alarmist. This time around, as I see the bulwarks of our democracy - the states, the courts and the people - protecting free and fair elections, I'm more optimistic. And people are saying I'm too optimistic. So let's hope that it goes that way.DAVIES: Well, Rick Hasen, thank you so much for speaking with us again.HASEN: It was great to be with you.DAVIES: Richard Hasen is director of the Safeguarding Democracy Project at the UCLA Law School. Since we recorded our conversation, there was another large political contribution. Michael Bloomberg gave $80 million to the Democrats. Coming up, we hear from Al Schmidt, chief election official in the swing state of Pennsylvania. This is FRESH AIR.(SOUNDBITE OF WES MONTGOMERY'S "4 ON 6")
